name: Lille score
seoDesc: Lille score: work out total score from the age and the creatinine. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Lille score calculator the age, the creatinine and the bilirubin and it returns total score. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Lille score calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lille score calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total score in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the age, the creatinine, the bilirubin (day 0) and the bilirubin (day 7).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in years.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in micromoles per liter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in micromoles per liter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lille score calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Albumin=((creatinine > 13 ÷ 10) ? ( (101 ÷ 147) × age + (23 ÷ 147) × bilirubin (day 0) − 11 ÷ 98 × bilirubin (day 7) + (16 ÷ 245) × PT + (1000 ÷ 147) × R + (206 ÷ 147) × (1) − 3190 ÷ 147 ) : ( (101 ÷ 147) × age + (23 ÷ 147) × bilirubin (day 0) − 11 ÷ 98 × bilirubin (day 7) + (16 ÷ 245) × PT + (1000 ÷ 147) × R + (206 ÷ 147) × (0) − 3190 ÷ 147 ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in grams per liter, and convertible to any of the 2 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Creatinine, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Albumin units, opening in grams per liter
  • Bilirubin, opening in micromoles per liter
  • Bilirubin, opening in micromoles per liter

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lille score calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the age, the creatinine and the bilirubin — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Lille score calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total score, derived from the age, the creatinine and the bilirubin. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lille score calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the creatinine and the bilirubin, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter PT in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. PT opens in seconds and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Lille score calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
